claim: In rat hippocampal neurons, an intracellular pool of the tetraspanin TSPAN5 promotes exocytosis of AMPA receptors without affecting their internalisation.
source: We found that, in rat hippocampal neurons, an intracellular pool of the tetraspanin TSPAN5 promotes exocytosis of AMPA receptors without affecting their internalisation.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data from multiple assays including surface staining, BS3 crosslinking, FRAP-FLIP experiments, and antibody-feeding assays showing TSPAN5's effect on AMPAR exocytosis but not internalization.

claim: TSPAN5 mediates its function by interacting with the adaptor protein complex AP4 and Stargazin.
source: TSPAN5 mediates this function by interacting with the adaptor protein complex AP4 and Stargazin and possibly using recycling endosomes as a delivery route.
evidence: The manuscript presents yeast two-hybrid screening, GST pulldown, co-immunoprecipitation, and proximity ligation assay data demonstrating interactions between TSPAN5, AP4, and Stargazin.

claim: TSPAN5 possibly uses recycling endosomes as a delivery route for AMPA receptors.
source: TSPAN5 mediates this function by interacting with the adaptor protein complex AP4 and Stargazin and possibly using recycling endosomes as a delivery route.
evidence: The manuscript presents vesicle fractionation data and colocalization studies with Rab11 (recycling endosome marker) suggesting TSPAN5 localizes to recycling endosomes, though the claim is stated as 'possibly' indicating some uncertainty.

claim: Tetraspanins are transmembrane proteins conserved in metazoans that present four transmembrane domains, a small and a large extracellular loop, and intracellular N- and C-termini.
source: Tetraspanins are transmembrane proteins conserved in metazoans that present four transmembrane domains, a small and a large extracellular loop, and intracellular N- and C-termini (Berditchevski, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Berditchevski, 2001, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Tetraspanins have the ability to organise tetraspanin enriched microdomains, membrane domains in which they accumulate.
source: Tetraspanins have the peculiar ability to organise tetraspanin enriched microdomains, membrane domains in which they accumulate (Charrin et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Charrin et al., 2002.

claim: Tetraspanins function as molecular facilitators by promoting physical proximity between proteins that belong to signalling complexes.
source: Tetraspanins have been proposed to function as molecular facilitators by promoting physical proximity between proteins that belong to signalling complexes (Charrin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Charrin et al., 2014 and represents a proposed mechanism.

claim: 33 tetraspanins have been described in mammals.
source: To date, 33 tetraspanins have been described in mammals, with functions in cell-cell adhesion, sperm-egg fusion, cell motility, and proliferation (Hemler, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hemler, 2005.

claim: Tetraspanins have functions in cell-cell adhesion, sperm-egg fusion, cell motility, and proliferation.
source: To date, 33 tetraspanins have been described in mammals, with functions in cell-cell adhesion, sperm-egg fusion, cell motility, and proliferation (Hemler, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hemler, 2005.

claim: TSPAN5 is part of the C8 subgroup of tetraspanins.
source: TSPAN5 is part of the C8 subgroup of tetraspanins and was previously shown to regulate the intracellular trafficking and activity of the protease ADAM-10 (Dornier et al., 2012; Eschenbrenner et al., 2020; Haining et al., 2012; Jouannet et al., 2016; Noy et al., 2016; Saint-Pol et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a classification statement that is presented as established knowledge.

claim: TSPAN5 was previously shown to regulate the intracellular trafficking and activity of the protease ADAM-10.
source: TSPAN5 is part of the C8 subgroup of tetraspanins and was previously shown to regulate the intracellular trafficking and activity of the protease ADAM-10 (Dornier et al., 2012; Eschenbrenner et al., 2020; Haining et al., 2012; Jouannet et al., 2016; Noy et al., 2016; Saint-Pol et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Dornier et al., 2012; Eschenbrenner et al., 2020; Haining et al., 2012; Jouannet et al., 2016; Noy et al., 2016; Saint-Pol et al., 2017).

claim: In hippocampal pyramidal neurons, TSPAN5 is enriched in dendritic spines and promotes their morphological maturation during synaptogenesis.
source: A previous study from our laboratory showed that, in hippocampal pyramidal neurons, TSPAN5 is enriched in dendritic spines and promotes their morphological maturation during synaptogenesis (Moretto et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors (Moretto et al., 2019).

claim: TSPAN5's action on dendritic spine maturation is mediated by controlling the surface mobility of the postsynaptic adhesion molecule neuroligin-1 via an interaction occurring on the plasma membrane.
source: This action is mediated by controlling the surface mobility of the postsynaptic adhesion molecule neuroligin-1 via an interaction occurring on the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim refers to findings from the previous study mentioned in the context, representing cited knowledge.

claim: A few studies have investigated the function of tetraspanins at the synapse identifying their role in intracellular trafficking of neurotransmitter receptors in neurons.
source: A few other studies have investigated the function of tetraspanins at the synapse identifying their role in intracellular trafficking of neurotransmitter receptors in neurons (Bassani et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2017; Murru et al., 2018; Murru et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Bassani et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2017; Murru et al., 2018; Murru et al., 2017).

claim: There is a significant increase in the intracellular pool of TSPAN5 in dendritic spines upon neuronal maturation.
source: Here, we report a significant increase in the intracellular pool of TSPAN5 in dendritic spines upon neuronal maturation.
evidence: This claim is supported by BS3 crosslinking experiments shown in Figure 1A demonstrating increased intracellular TSPAN5 from DIV12 to DIV19.

claim: In mature neurons TSPAN5 does not participate in dendritic spine maturation but has the main function of controlling surface delivery of AMPARs.
source: We demonstrate that in mature neurons TSPAN5 does not participate in dendritic spine maturation but has the main function of controlling surface delivery of α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) receptors (AMPARs).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1B showing minimal effects on spine morphology when TSPAN5 is knocked down at DIV13, and by multiple experiments showing effects on AMPAR surface levels.

claim: AMPARs are tetrameric complexes that mediate most of the fast excitatory transmission in response to the neurotransmitter glutamate in neurons.
source: AMPARs are tetrameric complexes that mediate most of the fast excitatory transmission in response to the neurotransmitter glutamate in neurons (Henley and Wilkinson, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Henley and Wilkinson, 2016 and represents established knowledge.

claim: AMPAR surface levels are directly responsible for synapse weakening or strengthening during synaptic plasticity.
source: AMPAR surface levels are directly responsible for synapse weakening or strengthening during synaptic plasticity (Huganir and Nicoll, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Huganir and Nicoll, 2013.

claim: AMPAR intracellular trafficking is an extremely complex phenomenon involving several auxiliary proteins.
source: their intracellular trafficking is an extremely complex phenomenon involving several auxiliary proteins (Anggono and Huganir, 2012; Moretto and Passafaro, 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Anggono and Huganir, 2012 and Moretto and Passafaro, 2018.

claim: AMPAR trafficking can be impaired in neurological and neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: that can be impaired in neurological and neurodevelopmental disorders (Henley and Wilkinson, 2016; Moretto et al., 2016; Moretto et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Henley and Wilkinson, 2016; Moretto et al., 2016; Moretto et al., 2018.

claim: AP4 is a member of the adaptor protein complex family.
source: Importantly, we found that TSPAN5 exerts this function by interacting with AP4, a member of the adaptor protein complex family (Boehm and Bonifacino, 2001; Bonifacino, 2014; Robinson and Bonifacino, 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boehm and Bonifacino, 2001; Bonifacino, 2014; Robinson and Bonifacino, 2001.

claim: Genes coding for AP4 are mutated in a syndrome characterised by spastic paraplegia and intellectual disability.
source: which coding genes are mutated in a syndrome characterised by spastic paraplegia and intellectual disability (Sanger et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sanger et al., 2019.

claim: AP4 was previously found to regulate the intracellular trafficking and sorting of several transmembrane proteins in neurons including the stargazin-AMPARs complex.
source: AP4 was previously found to regulate the intracellular trafficking and sorting of several transmembrane proteins in neurons including the stargazin-AMPARs complex (Matsuda et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Matsuda et al., 2008.

claim: AP4 was previously found to regulate the intracellular trafficking and sorting of the glutamate receptor δ2.
source: AP4 was previously found to regulate the intracellular trafficking and sorting of several transmembrane proteins in neurons including the stargazin-AMPARs complex (Matsuda et al., 2008), the glutamate receptor δ2 (Yap et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yap et al., 2003.

claim: AMPARs defective trafficking is a possible mechanism for intellectual disability symptoms in the AP4 deficiency syndrome.
source: Our data identify a novel function of TSPAN5 at the synapse and highlight AMPARs defective trafficking as a possible mechanism for intellectual disability symptoms in the AP4 deficiency syndrome.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the authors' findings connecting TSPAN5, AP4, and AMPAR trafficking, inferred from their experimental data.

claim: TSPAN5 appears as a complex pattern of bands on western blots, probably due to the association of this protein with cholesterol-rich membranes which makes it poorly soluble in standard lysis buffers.
source: As shown in Figure 1A, TSPAN5 appears as a complex pattern of bands. This is probably due to the association of this protein with cholesterol-rich membranes which makes it poorly soluble in standard lysis buffers (Charrin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and a citation to Charrin et al., 2014 explaining the biochemical behavior.

claim: All TSPAN5 bands observed on western blots are specific.
source: We previously demonstrated that all these bands are specific (Moretto et al., 2019) and thus they were all included in the quantification.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work (Moretto et al., 2019).

claim: There is an increase in the intracellular levels of TSPAN5 from DIV12 to DIV19.
source: We observed an increase in the intracellular levels of TSPAN5 from DIV12 to DIV19, which was not accompanied by a concomitant increase in plasma membrane levels (Figure 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by BS3 crosslinking data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The increase in intracellular levels of TSPAN5 from DIV12 to DIV19 was not accompanied by a concomitant increase in plasma membrane levels.
source: We observed an increase in the intracellular levels of TSPAN5 from DIV12 to DIV19, which was not accompanied by a concomitant increase in plasma membrane levels (Figure 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by BS3 crosslinking data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Increased intracellular levels of TSPAN5 do not necessarily imply increased delivery of this protein to the plasma membrane.
source: suggesting that increased intracellular levels of TSPAN5 do not necessarily imply increased delivery of this protein to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that intracellular TSPAN5 increases without corresponding plasma membrane increase.

claim: The transferrin receptor showed a more stable distribution across DIV12 and DIV19 time points.
source: The transferrin receptor showed a more stable distribution across these time points.
evidence: This claim is supported by the BS3 crosslinking data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Dendritic spine density was reduced by approximately 20% when TSPAN5 was knocked down at DIV13.
source: We analysed dendritic spine density and morphology at DIV21 (Figure 1B) and observed that dendritic spine density was reduced, but to a lower extent compared to our previous observations when knocking down TSPAN5 at DIV5 (20% compared to more than 65% reduction, respectively) (Moretto et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1B and comparison to previous work.

claim: The morphology of dendritic spines was completely unaffected by TSPAN5 knockdown at DIV13.
source: Even more interestingly, the morphology of dendritic spines was completely unaffected by TSPAN5 knockdown at this time point.
evidence: This claim is supported by the morphology analysis shown in Figure 1B pie charts.

claim: When TSPAN5 levels were downregulated from DIV5, there was a strong reduction (50%) in mature mushroom dendritic spines in favour of less mature thin dendritic spines.
source: In contrast, our previous results had shown a strong reduction (50%) in mature mushroom dendritic spines in favour of less mature thin dendritic spines when TSPAN5 levels were downregulated from DIV5 (Moretto et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work (Moretto et al., 2019).

claim: TSPAN5 has a more prominent role for dendritic spine maturation at early stages of development.
source: These data support a more prominent role of TSPAN5 for dendritic spine maturation at early stages of development and suggest that TSPAN5 might be involved in other functions at more mature stages.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the effects of TSPAN5 knockdown at different developmental stages.

claim: TSPAN5 might be involved in other functions at more mature stages of neuronal development.
source: These data support a more prominent role of TSPAN5 for dendritic spine maturation at early stages of development and suggest that TSPAN5 might be involved in other functions at more mature stages.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the differential effects observed at different developmental stages.

claim: The C-terminus of other tetraspanins has been shown to regulate the intracellular trafficking of other proteins.
source: The C-terminus of other tetraspanins has been shown to regulate the intracellular trafficking of other proteins (Bassani et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bassani et al., 2012.

claim: Four clones from the yeast two-hybrid screen coded for amino acids 1–102 of the protein AP4σ.
source: Among the clones identified (the full list is presented in Figure 2—source data 1), four of them coded for amino acids 1–102 of the protein AP4σ, one of the subunits of the adaptor protein complex AP4 (Boehm and Bonifacino, 2001; Bonifacino, 2014; Robinson and Bonifacino, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid screening data.

claim: AP4σ is one of the subunits of the adaptor protein complex AP4.
source: four of them coded for amino acids 1–102 of the protein AP4σ, one of the subunits of the adaptor protein complex AP4 (Boehm and Bonifacino, 2001; Bonifacino, 2014; Robinson and Bonifacino, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boehm and Bonifacino, 2001; Bonifacino, 2014; Robinson and Bonifacino, 2001.

claim: The AP4 complex is an obligate tetramer of four different subunits (β, µ, ε, and σ).
source: This complex is an obligate tetramer of four different subunits (β, µ, ε, and σ), which readily assemble and are almost undetectable as single subunits (Hirst et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hirst et al., 2013.

claim: The AP4 complex subunits readily assemble and are almost undetectable as single subunits.
source: This complex is an obligate tetramer of four different subunits (β, µ, ε, and σ), which readily assemble and are almost undetectable as single subunits (Hirst et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hirst et al., 2013.

claim: The AP4 complex has been previously shown to participate in intracellular trafficking of transmembrane proteins, including AMPARs via direct interaction of its epsilon subunit with the auxiliary AMPAR subunit Stargazin.
source: The AP4 complex has been previously shown to participate in intracellular trafficking of transmembrane proteins, including AMPARs via direct interaction of its epsilon subunit with the auxiliary AMPAR subunit Stargazin (Matsuda et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Matsuda et al., 2008.

claim: The C-terminus of TSPAN5 fused to GST precipitated AP4ε from rat brain lysates.
source: We validated the interaction between TSPAN5 and AP4 by GST pulldown on rat brain lysates (cortices and hippocampi) using the C-terminus of TSPAN5 fused to GST (GST-Ct) which precipitated AP4ε (Figure 2A), one of the subunits of the AP4 complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pulldown data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: TSPAN5, AP4σ, and AP4ε are associated as demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation from rat brain lysates.
source: In addition, we confirmed the interaction via co-immunoprecipitation experiments by immunoprecipitating TSPAN5, AP4σ, or AP4ε from rat brain lysates (cortices and hippocampi) and found that all three proteins were associated (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The C-terminal tail of TSPAN5 is sufficient to precipitate Stargazin, GluA1, and GluA2/3.
source: By using the C-terminus of TSPAN5 for GST-pulldown experiments on rat brain lysates, we were able to confirm that the C-terminal tail of TSPAN5 is sufficient to precipitate Stargazin, GluA1, and GluA2/3 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pulldown data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The NMDA receptor subunit GluN2A was not detected in the precipitates with TSPAN5 C-terminus, supporting the specificity of the interaction.
source: The NMDA receptor subunit GluN2A instead was not detected in the precipitates, supporting the specificity of the interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by the GST pulldown data shown in Figure 2C where GluN2A is not detected.

claim: GluA2/3 appeared to be pulled down more efficiently than GluA1 by TSPAN5 C-terminus, suggesting a preferential association between TSPAN5 and GluA2/3-containing AMPARs.
source: Interestingly, GluA2/3 appeared to be pulled down more efficiently than GluA1, suggesting a preferential association between TSPAN5 and GluA2/3-containing AMPARs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of GST pulldown data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The C-terminal tail of Stargazin was previously identified to be the region responsible for the interaction with AP4.
source: To further characterise the interaction, we performed GST pulldown using the C-terminal tail of Stargazin, which was previously identified to be the region responsible for the interaction with AP4 (Matsuda et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Matsuda et al., 2008.

claim: GST-Ct-Stargazin precipitated GluA2/3 and TSPAN5 but not CD81.
source: With this experiment, we detected GluA2/3 and TSPAN5 in the precipitate (Figure 2E). As a negative control, CD81, another member of the tetraspanin family, was not precipitated by the GST-Ct-Stargazin.
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pulldown data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The formation of the complex between TSPAN5, Stargazin, and GluA2 was confirmed in immunoprecipitation experiments in Hela cells transfected with TSPAN5-GFP, Stargazin-HA, and GluA2.
source: The formation of the complex was also confirmed in immunoprecipitation experiments in Hela cells, which endogenously express AP4, transfected with TSPAN5-GFP, Stargazin-HA, and GluA2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: TSPAN5 is not necessary for the formation of the AP4-Stargazin-AMPAR complex.
source: This suggests that TSPAN5 is not necessary for the formation of the complex
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the complex forms in cells without TSPAN5.

claim: TSPAN5 could be involved in directing the AP4-Stargazin-AMPAR complex to the correct organelle for its delivery to the plasma membrane.
source: and we hypothesised that it could be participating in directing these proteins to a specific cellular compartment.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: AP4ε, TSPAN5, Stargazin, GluA1, and GluA2/3 are all present at significant levels in the heaviest fractions of a sucrose gradient which are positive for the recycling endosomes marker transferrin receptor.
source: We observed that AP4ε, TSPAN5, Stargazin, GluA1, and GluA2/3 are all present at significant levels in the heaviest fractions which are positive for the recycling endosomes marker transferrin receptor (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by vesicle fractionation data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The intracellular pool of TSPAN5 could associate with AP4, Stargazin, GluA1, and GluA2 in recycling endosomes.
source: This experiment suggests that the intracellular pool of TSPAN5 could associate with AP4, Stargazin, GluA1, and GluA2 in recycling endosomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cofractionation data showing these proteins in transferrin receptor-positive fractions.

claim: TSPAN5 showed a high level of colocalisation with Rab4, Rab7, and Rab11.
source: TSPAN5 showed a high level of colocalisation with all three Rabs.
evidence: This claim is supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Colocalisation of TSPAN5 with Rab11-positive endosomes was significantly higher than with Rab4 or Rab7.
source: However, colocalisation with Rab11-positive endosomes was significantly higher than with the other two Rabs.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of colocalization data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Colocalisation of PLA signal between TSPAN5 and GluA2 was more pronounced with Rab11 than with Rab5 or Rab7.
source: Although some level of colocalisation was visible with all three Rabs, this was more pronounced with Rab11 (Figure 3D), strongly pointing towards Rab11-positive organelles as the location in which the complex between TSPAN5, AP4, Stargazin, and AMPARs preferentially forms.
evidence: This claim is supported by PLA colocalization data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Rab11-positive organelles are the location in which the complex between TSPAN5, AP4, Stargazin, and AMPARs preferentially forms.
source: Although some level of colocalisation was visible with all three Rabs, this was more pronounced with Rab11 (Figure 3D), strongly pointing towards Rab11-positive organelles as the location in which the complex between TSPAN5, AP4, Stargazin, and AMPARs preferentially forms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the higher colocalization of TSPAN5-GluA2 PLA signal with Rab11 compared to other Rabs.

claim: Knockdown of TSPAN5 induced a reduction of surface GluA2 levels that was reversed in the rescue condition.
source: We observed that knockdown of TSPAN5 induced a reduction of surface GluA2 levels that was reversed in the rescue condition (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by surface staining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: GluA1 appeared to be increased upon TSPAN5 knockdown, an effect that was reversed in the rescue condition.
source: In contrast, GluA1 appeared to be increased upon TSPAN5 knockdown (Figure 4B), an effect that was reversed in the rescue condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by surface staining data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The reduction of GluA2 and the increase in GluA1 upon TSPAN5 knockdown were present in both dendritic spines and dendritic shafts.
source: The reduction of GluA2 and the increase in GluA1 were present in both compartments (Figure 4A and B), suggesting that these effects are not restricted to dendritic spines.
evidence: This claim is supported by compartment-specific analysis shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The effects of TSPAN5 knockdown on GluA2 and GluA1 are not restricted to dendritic spines.
source: The reduction of GluA2 and the increase in GluA1 were present in both compartments (Figure 4A and B), suggesting that these effects are not restricted to dendritic spines.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that effects occur in both spines and shafts.

claim: BS3 crosslinking experiments showed a significant reduction in plasma membrane and total levels of GluA2/3 upon TSPAN5 knockdown.
source: In these experiments, we observed a significant reduction in plasma membrane and total levels of GluA2/3, possibly suggesting an increased degradation of the receptor in addition to its reduced plasma membrane localisation.
evidence: This claim is supported by BS3 crosslinking data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The reduction in GluA2/3 levels upon TSPAN5 knockdown possibly suggests an increased degradation of the receptor in addition to its reduced plasma membrane localisation.
source: In these experiments, we observed a significant reduction in plasma membrane and total levels of GluA2/3, possibly suggesting an increased degradation of the receptor in addition to its reduced plasma membrane localisation.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation of reduced total levels.

claim: The increase in GluA1 upon TSPAN5 knockdown was observed both in the plasma membrane fraction and in the total level.
source: Similarly, the increase in GluA1 was observed both in the plasma membrane fraction and in the total level, suggesting a potential compensatory effect driven by increased protein synthesis or reduced degradation.
evidence: This claim is supported by BS3 crosslinking data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The increase in GluA1 upon TSPAN5 knockdown suggests a potential compensatory effect driven by increased protein synthesis or reduced degradation.
source: Similarly, the increase in GluA1 was observed both in the plasma membrane fraction and in the total level, suggesting a potential compensatory effect driven by increased protein synthesis or reduced degradation.
evidence: This is a speculative inference to explain the observed increase in GluA1.

claim: TSPAN5-ΔC (lacking the C-terminus) was unable to rescue the knockdown of TSPAN5 in terms of GluA2 surface levels.
source: We found that the TSPAN5- ΔC was unable to rescue the knockdown of TSPAN5, confirming the importance of the TSPAN5-AP4 interaction for maintaining the correct surface levels of GluA2.
evidence: This claim is supported by surface staining data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The TSPAN5-AP4 interaction is important for maintaining the correct surface levels of GluA2.
source: We found that the TSPAN5- ΔC was unable to rescue the knockdown of TSPAN5, confirming the importance of the TSPAN5-AP4 interaction for maintaining the correct surface levels of GluA2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the failure of the C-terminus deletion mutant to rescue the phenotype.

claim: Targeting one subunit of AP4 reduced the expression also of the other subunits.
source: In line with previous findings (Matsuda et al., 2008; Hirst et al., 2013), targeting one subunit reduced the expression also of the others.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR and western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: The knockdown of either AP4 or TSPAN5 reduced GluA2 surface levels to the same extent.
source: We analysed GluA2 surface levels at DIV20 and observed that the knockdown of either AP4 or TSPAN5 reduced GluA2 levels to the same extent.
evidence: This claim is supported by surface staining data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The simultaneous knockdown of TSPAN5 and AP4 did not induce any further reduction in GluA2 surface levels beyond single knockdowns.
source: In addition, the simultaneous knockdown of TSPAN5 and AP4 did not induce any further reduction (Figure 5C), supporting the hypothesis that the two proteins participate in the same pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by surface staining data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: TSPAN5 and AP4 participate in the same pathway for regulating GluA2 surface levels.
source: In addition, the simultaneous knockdown of TSPAN5 and AP4 did not induce any further reduction (Figure 5C), supporting the hypothesis that the two proteins participate in the same pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of additive effect when both proteins are knocked down.

claim: Reducing AP4 levels compromised the interaction between TSPAN5 and GluA2.
source: As expected, reducing AP4 levels compromised the interaction between TSPAN5 and GluA2.
evidence: This claim is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: TSPAN7 was previously shown to regulate AMPAR internalisation.
source: Another tetraspanin, TSPAN7, was previously shown to regulate AMPAR internalisation (Bassani et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bassani et al., 2012.

claim: Both scrambled- and Sh-TSPAN5-transfected neurons exhibited a significant increase in the GluA2 intracellular/total ratio after 5 min of antibody incubation.
source: Both scrambled- and Sh-TSPAN5-transfected neurons exhibited a significant increase in the GluA2 intracellular/total ratio after 5 min, suggesting that AMPAR internalisation is not affected by TSPAN5 knockdown.
evidence: This claim is supported by antibody-feeding assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: AMPAR internalisation is not affected by TSPAN5 knockdown.
source: Both scrambled- and Sh-TSPAN5-transfected neurons exhibited a significant increase in the GluA2 intracellular/total ratio after 5 min, suggesting that AMPAR internalisation is not affected by TSPAN5 knockdown.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar internalization kinetics in control and TSPAN5 knockdown conditions.

claim: In scrambled-transfected neurons, recycling of GluA2 at 10 min post incubation brought the receptor back to the surface, with levels of the intracellular/total ratio similar to those at time point 0.
source: Interestingly, in scrambled-transfected neurons, recycling of the receptor at 10 min post incubation brought GluA2 back to the surface, with levels of the intracellular/total ratio similar to those at time point 0
evidence: This claim is supported by antibody-feeding assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Sh-TSPAN5-transfected neurons maintained higher levels of internalised GluA2 at the 10 min time point.
source: by contrast, the Sh-TSPAN5-transfected neurons maintained higher levels of internalised receptor at the 10 min time point.
evidence: This claim is supported by antibody-feeding assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The maintained internalization of GluA2 in TSPAN5 knockdown neurons potentially points to defects in GluA2 exocytosis.
source: This potentially points to defects in GluA2 exocytosis.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation that internalized receptors don't return to the surface as efficiently.

claim: Recycling levels of endogenous GluA2 receptors are too low to be detected by an antibody-feeding approach.
source: To this end, we relied on an overexpression model as recycling levels of endogenous GluA2 receptors are too low to be detected by an antibody-feeding approach.
evidence: This is a statement about technical limitations based on the authors' knowledge and experience.

claim: SEP is only fluorescent at a neutral pH, allowing for the visualisation of the receptor only when it is exposed to the neutral extracellular environment.
source: SEP is extremely useful for intracellular trafficking studies as it is only fluorescent at a neutral pH, allowing for the visualisation of the receptor only when it is exposed to the neutral extracellular environment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the properties of SEP, supported by the verification experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: SEP fluorescence is quenched in acidic intracellular vesicles.
source: Instead, its fluorescence is quenched in the acidic intracellular vesicles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SEP properties, verified by experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Individual dendritic spines are virtually devoid of endoplasmic reticulum.
source: To avoid interferences from endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-contained GluA2, we only evaluated the signal in individual dendritic spines, which are virtually devoid of ER (Rathje et al., 2013; Rathje et al., 2014; Wilkinson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rathje et al., 2013; Rathje et al., 2014; Wilkinson et al., 2014.

claim: There were no differences in the levels or kinetics of SEP-GluA2 recycling between scrambled-, Sh-TSPAN5-, or rescue mCherry-transfected neurons when cycloheximide was applied.
source: To our surprise, there were no differences in the levels or kinetics of SEP-GluA2 recycling between scrambled-, Sh-TSPAN5-, or rescue mCherry-transfected neurons (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP-FLIP data with cycloheximide shown in Figure 6B–D.

claim: A significant reduction of the recovery after photobleaching in individual dendritic spines was observed in Sh-TSPAN5-transfected neurons compared to scrambled-transfected neurons when cycloheximide was not applied.
source: In this experiment, we observed a significant reduction of the recovery after photobleaching in individual dendritic spines of Sh-TSPAN5-transfected neurons compared to scrambled-transfected neurons as measured by the area under the curve (Figure 6F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP-FLIP data without cycloheximide shown in Figure 6F–H.

claim: Sh-TSPAN5 neurons presented smaller steady state ΔF/Fpre (parameter A) and greater time constant τ compared to scrambled condition, suggesting lower steady-state recovery of GluA2 and slower kinetics.
source: For both parameters the Sh-TSPAN5 neurons presented significant differences compared to the scrambled condition with smaller A and greater τ, suggesting lower steady-state recovery of GluA2 and slower kinetics (Figure 6I).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic analysis of FRAP-FLIP data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Exocytosis of newly synthesised GluA2 receptors is regulated by TSPAN5.
source: These data strongly suggest that exocytosis of newly synthesised GluA2 receptors is regulated by TSPAN5.
evidence: This is an inference based on the FRAP-FLIP experiments showing effects only when protein synthesis is not blocked.

claim: TSPAN5 could also regulate the recycling of GluA2-containing AMPARs, an effect that would be masked by the application of cycloheximide.
source: However, our experiments do not exclude the possibility that TSPAN5 could also regulate the recycling of GluA2-containing AMPARs, an effect that would be masked by the application of cycloheximide in the experiment presented in Figure 6A–D which could cause the loss of rapidly turning over factors needed for this process.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging limitations of the experimental approach.

claim: TSPAN5 knockdown resulted in a reduction in the surface levels of ARIAD-GluA2 90 min after application of the ARIAD ligand.
source: As expected from our previous results, TSPAN5 knockdown resulted in a reduction in the surface levels of ARIAD-GluA2 90 min after application of the ARIAD ligand, an effect that was rescued by re-expression of the Sh-resistant form of TSPAN5 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ARIAD-GluA2 surface staining data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: No change was detected in the average speed of transport of GluA2-containing vesicles in either the anterograde or retrograde direction upon TSPAN5 knockdown.
source: Here, we did not detect any change in the average speed of transport of GluA2-containing vesicles in either the anterograde or retrograde direction (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B)
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data of ARIAD-tdTomato-GluA2 transport shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: No change was detected in the average number of GluA2-containing vesicles upon TSPAN5 knockdown.
source: nor in the average number of vesicles (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of vesicle numbers shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There is either a lower amount of GluA2 loaded into vesicles directed for exocytosis or these vesicles fail to deliver their content to the plasma membrane and might be directed for degradation upon TSPAN5 knockdown.
source: These results suggest that there is either a lower amount of GluA2 loaded into each of these vesicles directed for exocytosis or that these vesicles fail to deliver their content to the plasma membrane of dendrites and might be directed for degradation as a result.
evidence: This is a speculative inference to explain the reduced surface levels despite normal vesicle transport.

claim: Leupeptin treatment increased GluA2/3 to similar levels in scrambled- and Sh-TSPAN5-transfected neurons.
source: Leupeptin treatment increased GluA2/3 to similar levels in scrambled- and Sh-TSPAN5-transfected neurons, suggesting that AMPARs degradation is increased in the absence of TSPAN5 (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data with leupeptin treatment shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: AMPARs degradation is increased in the absence of TSPAN5.
source: Leupeptin treatment increased GluA2/3 to similar levels in scrambled- and Sh-TSPAN5-transfected neurons, suggesting that AMPARs degradation is increased in the absence of TSPAN5 (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the leupeptin rescue experiment.

claim: AMPARs are mostly degraded via the lysosomal pathway.
source: To test this second possibility, we assessed the total levels of GluA2/3 via immunofluorescence in DIV20 neurons transfected at DIV12 with either scrambled or Sh-TSPAN5 and treated with the lysosomal inhibitor leupeptin (Figure 7D and E), since AMPARs are mostly degraded via this pathway (Ehlers, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ehlers, 2000.

claim: Silencing TSPAN5 reduced the surface levels of newly synthesised GluA1, which was rescued by re-expressing an ShRNA-resistant TSPAN5.
source: Silencing TSPAN5 also reduced the surface levels of newly synthesised GluA1, which was rescued by re-expressing an ShRNA-resistant TSPAN5.
evidence: This claim is supported by ARIAD-GluA1 surface staining data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The overall increase in the surface GluA1 levels upon TSPAN5 knockdown is a compensatory mechanism.
source: This strengthen the hypothesis that the overall increase in the surface GluA1 levels (Figure 4B–D) is a compensatory mechanism.
evidence: This is a speculative inference to reconcile the different effects on newly synthesized vs. steady-state GluA1 levels.

claim: The association of TSPAN5 with GluA2, occurring via AP4 and Stargazin, promotes the exocytosis of AMPARs, potentially via Rab11/TfR-positive recycling endosomes.
source: Altogether, our data support a model whereby the association of TSPAN5 with GluA2, occurring via AP4 and Stargazin, promotes the exocytosis of AMPARs, potentially via Rab11/TfR-positive recycling endosomes (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a summary model integrating multiple experimental findings from the study.

claim: The intracellular pool of TSPAN5 participates in the delivery of newly synthesised AMPARs to the plasma membrane.
source: In this work, we have identified an intracellular pool of TSPAN5 that participates in the delivery of newly synthesised AMPARs to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding, supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: TSPAN5 forms a complex with AP4, Stargazin, and AMPARs.
source: We showed that TSPAN5 forms a complex with AP4, Stargazin, and AMPARs and that this interaction could take place in recycling endosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple biochemical and imaging experiments showing interactions and colocalization.

claim: The interaction between TSPAN5, AP4, Stargazin, and AMPARs could take place in recycling endosomes.
source: We showed that TSPAN5 forms a complex with AP4, Stargazin, and AMPARs and that this interaction could take place in recycling endosomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on cofractionation and colocalization data with recycling endosome markers.

claim: Recycling endosomes have been shown to participate in a non-canonical secretory pathway where proteins synthesised in the dendritic ER are trafficked to an ER-Golgi intermediate compartment before being loaded to recycling endosomes for insertion in the plasma membrane.
source: Although the main function of recycling endosomes is to redirect endocytosed receptors back to the plasma membrane, they have also been shown to participate in a non-canonical secretory pathway. Proteins synthesised in the dendritic ER are trafficked to an ER-Golgi intermediate compartment before being loaded to recycling endosomes for insertion in the plasma membrane (Bowen et al., 2017; Hirling, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bowen et al., 2017 and Hirling, 2009.

claim: In the non-canonical secretory pathway, receptors would bypass the Golgi compartment, which is poorly present in dendrites and dendritic spines.
source: As a result, the receptors would bypass the Golgi compartment, which is poorly present in dendrites and dendritic spines.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dendritic compartmentalization.

claim: The molecular regulators of the non-canonical secretory pathway are not well defined.
source: The molecular regulators of this process are not well defined.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: TSPAN5 could also regulate the recycling of AMPARs in addition to newly synthesized receptors.
source: In addition, our experiments cannot fully exclude that TSPAN5 could also regulate the recycling of AMPARs. It is thus possible that TSPAN5 could modulate the delivery to the plasma membrane of both newly synthesised and recycling AMPARs.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging limitations of the experimental approaches used.

claim: TSPAN5 appears to regulate the exocytosis of both GluA2 and GluA1.
source: Although our experiments show a differential effect of TSPAN5 knockdown on surface levels of GluA2 and GluA1 at the steady state, TSPAN5 appears to regulate the exocytosis of both GluA2 and GluA1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ARIAD experiments showing effects on both subunits.

claim: Both GluA2 and GluA1 can interact with Stargazin.
source: This is in line with the fact that both can interact with Stargazin (Chen et al., 2000), and thus with AP4 and TSPAN5 (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2000 and data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The differences in steady state surface levels of GluA2 and GluA1 upon TSPAN5 knockdown could be due to a compensatory potentiation of a secretory pathway that does not rely on TSPAN5 and that is responsible for GluA1-containing AMPAR delivery.
source: The differences at the steady state could be due to a compensatory potentiation of a secretory pathway that does not rely on TSPAN5 and that is responsible for GluA1-containing AMPAR delivery exploited to maintain normal synaptic activity.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed differential effects.

claim: GluA2 delivery and recycling is a constitutive process, whereas GluA1 exocytosis to the plasma membrane is more dependent on synaptic plasticity.
source: The trafficking of GluA2 and GluA1 was previously shown to be partially regulated by separate mechanisms for example with GluA2 delivery and recycling being a constitutive process, whereas GluA1 exocytosis to the plasma membrane is more dependent on synaptic plasticity (Passafaro et al., 2001; Shi et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Passafaro et al., 2001 and Shi et al., 2001.

claim: AMPAR-mediated mEPSCs are not affected by TSPAN5 knockdown in either their amplitude or frequency, but display altered kinetics.
source: This could partially explain our previous observation that AMPAR-mediated mEPSCs are not affected by TSPAN5 knockdown in either their amplitude or frequency, but display altered kinetics (Moretto et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work (Moretto et al., 2019).

claim: Altered kinetics of AMPAR-mediated mEPSCs can be due to a change in the receptor subunit composition.
source: which can be due to a change in the receptor subunit composition (Lu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lu et al., 2009.

claim: AP complexes select transmembrane proteins via interaction through typical sorting motifs and promote their insertion into specific vesicles.
source: AP complexes select transmembrane proteins via interaction through typical sorting motifs and promote their insertion into specific vesicles (Robinson, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Robinson, 2004.

claim: AP4 was found to restrict AMPARs from being directed towards the axonal compartment.
source: A role for AP4 in AMPARs intracellular trafficking was previously shown (Matsuda et al., 2008; Matsuda et al., 2013): AP4 was found to restrict AMPARs from being directed towards the axonal compartment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Matsuda et al., 2008 and Matsuda et al., 2013.

claim: AP4β knockout mice presented with mislocalisation of AMPARs to the axon, which accumulated in autophagosomes.
source: AP4β knockout mice presented with mislocalisation of AMPARs to the axon, which accumulated in autophagosomes.
evidence: This claim refers to findings from cited literature on AP4β knockout mice.

claim: Other AP complexes could compensate for the loss of AP4, particularly AP1 which was found to regulate sorting and exocytosis of membrane proteins.
source: It remains possible that other AP complexes could compensate for the loss of AP4. In particular, AP1 was found to regulate sorting and exocytosis of membrane proteins (Bonifacino, 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to Bonifacino, 2014.

claim: The involvement of AP4 in AMPAR exocytosis could potentially explain the intellectual disability phenotype of AP4 deficiency syndrome.
source: Interestingly, the involvement of AP4 in AMPAR exocytosis could potentially explain the intellectual disability phenotype of AP4 deficiency syndrome
evidence: This is a speculative inference connecting the authors' findings to clinical phenotypes.

claim: An imbalance between GluA2 and GluA1 subunits in the composition of AMPARs was previously shown to cause changes in how neurons respond to synaptic plasticity events, thus impacting on learning and memory functions.
source: an imbalance between GluA2 and GluA1 subunits in the composition of AMPARs was previously shown to cause changes in how neurons respond to synaptic plasticity events, thus impacting on learning and memory functions (Moretto et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Moretto et al., 2018.

claim: TSPAN5 is not necessary for the formation of the AP4-Stargazin-AMPAR complex but could be involved in directing the complex to the correct organelle for its delivery to the plasma membrane.
source: As the association between AP4, Stargazin, and AMPARs was shown to occur in heterologous cells, with little to no expression of TSPAN5 (Matsuda et al., 2008), we believe that TSPAN5 is not necessary for the formation of the complex but that it could rather be involved in directing the complex to the correct organelle for its delivery to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the complex forms without TSPAN5 in heterologous cells.

claim: TSPAN5 localisation at the plasma membrane is crucial for the maturation of dendritic spines during neuronal development.
source: Together with our previous work, these data highlight the importance of TSPAN5 for neuronal function. TSPAN5 appears to act on two independent pathways; on the one hand, its localisation at the plasma membrane is crucial for the maturation of dendritic spines during neuronal development (Moretto et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work (Moretto et al., 2019).

claim: TSPAN5 localisation in intracellular vesicles in mature neurons regulates exocytosis of AMPARs enabling correct synaptic function.
source: on the other hand, TSPAN5 localisation in intracellular vesicles in mature neurons regulates exocytosis of AMPARs enabling correct synaptic function.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings from the current study.

claim: At DIV19, primary neurons are considered functionally mature.
source: while at DIV19, primary neurons are considered functionally mature.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cultured neuron development.

claim: BS3 crosslinker is not permeable to membranes.
source: This crosslinker is not permeable to membranes and, as such, if applied to living cells will only crosslink plasma membrane proteins which will appear as high molecular weight bands upon western blot analysis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the properties of BS3 crosslinker.

claim: When BS3 is applied to living cells, it will only crosslink plasma membrane proteins which will appear as high molecular weight bands upon western blot analysis.
source: This crosslinker is not permeable to membranes and, as such, if applied to living cells will only crosslink plasma membrane proteins which will appear as high molecular weight bands upon western blot analysis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about how BS3 crosslinking works.

claim: The intracellular pool of proteins will not be crosslinked by BS3, thereby running at the expected molecular weight.
source: In contrast, the intracellular pool will not be crosslinked, thereby running at the expected molecular weight.
evidence: This is established knowledge about how BS3 crosslinking distinguishes intracellular from surface proteins.
